Getting started with /architect

You have just been given a login. This is what you will see, in the order you will meet it. It takes about ten minutes to read.

Karim Lameer, CodelessOps

Step 1 of 14

Sign in

I created your login and sent you a username and a password. There is no sign-up page, and nobody else can make a login.

Read the notice on the sign-in page once. It says what I can see as the person running this instance, and it says that what you upload is your responsibility. Upload only what you are allowed to share.

Step 2 of 14

Workspaces, Private and Shared

Everything lives in a workspace: a set of Anaplan models, their documents, your chats and your notes. Nothing is remembered from one workspace to the next.

A workspace is Private or Shared. Private is yours alone. Shared is open to everyone in your team, which means your company, and to nobody else. I never see inside either.

Step 3 of 14

Make a workspace from your Anaplan exports

You need up to three exports from each model. All three are grid exports from the model settings in Anaplan, saved as CSV.

You can start with Line Items alone. Add the other two when you can: answers about imports, exports and module sizes need them.

  • Line Items: in Anaplan, open Model Settings (the cog), then Line Items. Export the whole grid, all columns. This is the one that matters most: it holds every formula.
  • Modules: Model Settings, then Modules. Export the grid.
  • Actions: Model Settings, then Actions. Export each tab you use (Imports, Exports, Processes) or the combined grid.
  • One row per model on the new workspace page. Give each model the name your team calls it.
Step 4 of 14

Add your project documents

The exports say what was built. Your documents say why. Upload design records, meeting notes, handover notes, change requests: PDF, Word, Markdown or text.

Each document is split into sections, and each section is tied to the modules and line items it names. Nobody tags anything by hand. That link is what lets an answer quote the passage that records a decision.

Step 5 of 14

Ask a question

Type a question in plain words. Name the module or line item if you know it. If you do not, describe it and it will be found.

These eight are good first questions. Each one shows a different thing the tool can do.

Why is the account mapping written into the Forecast Opex formula instead of a lookup table?Cited documents, quote-checked
How is the depreciation charge calculated?The grammar: a formula read in parts and traced upstream
Build what change request CR-031 asks for: a legal fees driver in the opex forecast.A build plan with checked formulas and Planual flags
Give me an overview of the estate: what each model is for, who built it, and what a new builder must know.The model map
What should we fix first in FP&A, and what has already been decided?The review: ranked findings, Planual-tagged, with decisions already made on the cards
What are the implications of changing SYS05 FX Rates?Reach of a change
What do the project documents say about CAL03 Opex?Documents tied to objects at ingestion
Why is the margin module called CAL04 Margn?It says when it does not know
Step 6 of 14

Read an answer

An answer is short on purpose. The first lines are the answer. Then comes one picture or set of cards for that kind of question. Then the evidence.

A language model writes the words. Code checks them before you see them: every name against your exports, every figure against what was looked up, every quote against the document it cites.

Step 7 of 14

Concise and Full

Full gives the picture, the sources and the detail. Concise gives only what you act on, with the rest one click away.

Use Concise when you are in the middle of building and want the next step. Use Full when you are deciding.

Step 8 of 14

Build plans, and the Planual flags

Ask for a plan to build something and you get instructions you can follow in Anaplan: modules, line items, formats, formulas, in build order. Every formula is parsed and every name checked before the plan is shown. Nothing is built for you. It is a plan.

Each planned line item carries flags by Planual rule number: as per a rule, or departing from one. A flag is advice. You may have a good reason to depart, and often a document already records it.

When the plan needs something an export cannot hold, such as the name of a list member, it marks the gap as You supply and carries on.

Step 9 of 14

What a change touches

Before you change a line item or a module, ask what it reaches. You get every line item that reads it, counted once, by how many formulas away it is, with the actions and the other models involved.

Reach follows formula references. It tells you where to look. It does not prove a value will change.

Step 10 of 14

Notes: what you know that the model does not

A note is something you tell the tool once: why a module is kept, who owns a feed, what must not be touched. It is used in later answers and cited like a document.

Save any answer as a note from the button under it, or write one on the Notes page. A note is a working assumption until someone confirms it, and it says which it is.

Step 11 of 14

What it cannot see

It reads exports, so it knows what an export holds. Some things are not in any export, and it will say so when a question depends on them.

  • Pages, dashboards and saved views. It cannot tell you whether anyone looks at a line item.
  • List members. It knows a list exists and where it is used, not what is in it.
  • Data. No cell values, so it cannot tell you a number is wrong.
  • User access and selective access.
  • When nobody wrote a reason down, it says Not recorded. It does not guess.
Step 12 of 14

Your spend cap

Each question costs a little, because a language model answers it. Your login has a cap. A question counts against the cap of whoever asked it, in a shared workspace too.

When you reach the cap, the next question is refused with a plain message and nothing is lost. Message me and I will raise it.

Step 13 of 14

Tracing, and your choice

Tracing sends a record of a question and its answer to a separate service, so that I can see why an answer went wrong. For your login it is off unless you turn it on.

It is your choice alone, in Settings. A colleague turning it on does not send your questions anywhere, even in a chat you share.

Step 14 of 14

Who to ask

Me. Send me a message on LinkedIn: that is the one route, not email and not the website.

Tell me what you asked and what was wrong with the answer. If it is about access or a cap, say which login.
